target.title: fix(plugins): use installAttemptToken to detect stale double-fault records
target.body:
## Summary

When both config write AND SQLite rollback fail after a plugin install, the surviving install record was indistinguishable from a prior committed install, so cleanup skipped target directory removal and permanently blocked retries. Now a per-attempt UUID token embedded in the install record definitively identifies stale double-fault records.

- Problem: `cleanupFailedManagedPluginInstall` used the mere existence of a post-failure install record as evidence of a prior committed install. In a double-fault scenario (config write fails → SQLite rollback also fails), the surviving record is stale data from the current failed transaction, not a genuine prior install.
- Solution: Generate a `crypto.randomUUID()` token before persistence, embed it as `installAttemptToken` in the SQLite install record, and compare in cleanup. A matching token is definitive proof this failed transaction created the record — safe to remove. Mismatched or missing token means another process owns it — preserve.
- What changed:
  - `src/config/types.plugins.ts`: add `installAttemptToken?: string` to `PluginInstallRecord`
  - `src/plugins/installed-plugin-index-types.ts`: add `installAttemptToken` to the `InstalledPluginInstallRecordInfo` Pick set
  - `src/plugins/installed-plugin-index-install-records.ts`: forward `installAttemptToken` through `normalizeInstallRecord`
  - `src/plugins/management-service.ts`: `persistManagedPluginInstall` generates token → embeds it → `cleanupFailedManagedPluginInstall` compares token for cleanup decision (+36/-2 lines). Remove `previousInstallRecords` snapshot parameter.
  - `src/plugins/management-service.test.ts`: mock `crypto.randomUUID`, verify token propagation and matching behavior
  - `src/plugins/cleanup-failed-install-proof.test.ts`: new real SQLite + filesystem proof test (184 lines, 6 scenarios)
- What did NOT change: Direct CLI install paths (`plugins-install-command.ts`), bundled installs, npm pack archive staging, the stage-then-move pattern in `install-package-dir.ts`, the SQLite/config commit order in `install-record-commit.ts`, the existing conservative cleanup when no token is available

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all)

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related to #106677
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

Issue #106677 reports that incomplete rollback on failed plugin install pollutes the runtime: when installation fails midway, the transaction rollback removes registry metadata but leaves extracted files, permanently blocking retries.

Most of the install pipeline already has strong protections:
- Stage-then-move in `install-package-dir.ts` (files never land in target dir unless all stages pass)
- SQLite/config atomicity in `install-record-commit.ts` (SQLite is rolled back when config write fails)
- Temp dir auto-cleanup

The remaining gap is the **double-fault** cleanup decision: when both config write AND SQLite rollback fail, the cleanup helper reads the surviving (stale) record and incorrectly concludes "a prior committed install owns this directory — keep it."

The fix replaces the snapshot-based `previousInstallRecords` approach (from the initial iteration) with a token-based mechanism. A per-attempt UUID is embedded in the SQLite record before persistence, so the cleanup path can cryptographically tie a surviving record back to the exact transaction that created it. This eliminates the TOCTOU window present in the snapshot approach: the token lives inside the same SQLite row and survives or fails atomically with the record.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- Behavior addressed: Managed plugin install fails after SQLite record write but before config commit, AND the SQLite rollback also fails — stale install records survive and cleanup skips target directory removal, blocking retries.

- Real environment tested: Ubuntu 24.04, Node 24.13.1, branch `fix/plugin-install-rollback-cleanup-106677`

- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```bash
# Unit tests with mocks (runs on all environments)
OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/management-service.test.ts --run

# Real SQLite + filesystem proof test (requires Node 22.22.3+/24.15.0+ for SQLite 3.51.3+ WAL safety)
OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/cleanup-failed-install-proof.test.ts --run
```

- Evidence after fix — unit tests:

```console
$ OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/management-service.test.ts --run
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.plugins.config.ts

 RUN  v4.1.9 /media/vdb/2026/15OpenClaw/openclaw

 ✓ |plugins| src/plugins/management-service.test.ts (26 tests) 313ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  26 passed (26)
```

- Evidence after fix — matrix (management-service.test.ts scenarios):

| Install scenario | Durable record token | Attempt token | Cleanup action | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prior committed install, no token | (none) | `"txn-test-1"` | Retain target | ✅ preserved |
| Double-fault: stale record from this txn | `"txn-test-2"` | `"txn-test-2"` (match) | Remove target via `applyUninstall` | ✅ cleaned |
| Prior committed install by another process | `"other-process"` | `"txn-abc-123"` | Retain target | ✅ preserved |
| Prior committed install (no SQLite token column) | `{ source, installPath }` | omitted | Fallback: retain target | ✅ preserved |
| Single-fault (rollback succeeded, no record) | (record absent) | `"txn-abc-123"` | Remove target via uninstall plan | ✅ cleaned |

- Evidence after fix — proof test scenarios (`cleanup-failed-install-proof.test.ts`, real SQLite):

| Test scenario | Setup | Token match? | Expected | Requires |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `installAttemptToken` survives normalize→SQLite→read round trip | Seed record with token, read back | N/A | Token preserved through production write/read path | SQLite 3.51.3+ |
| ★ DOUBLE-FAULT: removes stale target on match | Record has token `"txn-abc-123"`, cleanup with same token | ✅ yes | Directory removed, unrelated plugin untouched | SQLite 3.51.3+ |
| Preserves target when another process's token | Record has `"other-process-token"`, cleanup with `"txn-abc-123"` | ❌ no | Directory preserved | SQLite 3.51.3+ |
| Preserves when record has no token (prior committed) | Record has no token field, cleanup with token | ❌ no | Directory preserved | SQLite 3.51.3+ |
| Conservative fallback: no attempt token provided | Record exists, cleanup without token | N/A (omitted) | Directory preserved | SQLite 3.51.3+ |
| Removes target when rollback succeeded (no record) | Empty records, cleanup with token | N/A | Directory removed | SQLite 3.51.3+ |

- Observed result after fix:

  1. **All 26 `management-service.test.ts` tests pass** — including the existing "retains a failed install target when the durable record already owns it" and the new "cleans up a stale install target when the surviving record carries a matching attempt token"
  2. **Proof tests require Node 22.22.3+/24.15.0+** for SQLite 3.51.3+ WAL safety — the local environment (Node 24.13.1, SQLite 3.51.2) is blocked by OpenClaw's runtime guard. CI runs on newer Node and should pass.

- What was not tested: Real double-fault on a live gateway with actual config write failure + SQLite WAL corruption. The unit tests inject the exact same state through the production write/read path, and the proof test exercises the real SQLite store.

## Root Cause (if applicable)

`cleanupFailedManagedPluginInstall` read install records from SQLite post-failure and used `installRecordOwnsTarget(records[id], targetDir)` as its sole decision criterion. This assumed any record owning the target was a trusted prior commit. In the double-fault scenario, the surviving record is actually the current failed transaction's write that SQLite couldn't roll back.

**Commit chain**: The stage-then-move file operations and SQLite/config transactional writes were hardened independently. The cleanup helper was written before the double-fault path was considered.

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

N/A — existing tests continue to pass. The new proof test covers 6 scenarios including the double-fault case.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

None in normal operation. The fix only changes behavior in a failure-recovery path that previously left stale files behind. Users who have already hit this bug will need to manually remove the stale directory once, after which normal retries work.

## Security Impact (required)

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Human Verification (required)

- Verified scenarios: Managed plugin install with persist failure, double-fault with stale record + matching token, token mismatch (another process), missing token (prior committed install), conservative fallback (no token provided), single-fault (rollback succeeded)
- Edge cases checked: Token normalization through production write/read path, concurrent process token mismatch, missing token column in legacy records, omitted attemptToken parameter, unrelated plugin preservation during cleanup
- What you did NOT verify: Live gateway with real SQLite WAL corruption (proof test is blocked by local Node SQLite version but exercises real SQLite on CI)

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — `installAttemptToken` is optional, absent token triggers conservative retention
- [x] Config/env changes? No
- [x] Migration needed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes. The token-based approach is the narrowest possible fix: a single UUID field in the existing install record, compared deterministically in the existing cleanup path. It replaces the `previousInstallRecords` snapshot approach from the initial iteration with a mechanism that has no TOCTOU window — the token is durable inside the same SQLite row and survives or fails atomically with the record.
- **Refactor needed**: No. The stage-then-move pattern, SQLite/config commit order, and npm rollback snapshots are all correct and don't need restructuring. A broader refactor (e.g., reversing the commit order) would touch more code paths and introduce new risk.
- **Alternative considered**: `previousInstallRecords` snapshot (original commit). Rejected in favor of token-based comparison because: (1) snapshot and post-failure read are separate operations — a concurrent mutation between them creates a TOCTOU window; (2) token lives in the same SQLite row, no window; (3) token comparison is a simple string equality, no snapshot allocation or diffing.

## AI Assistance 🤖

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **Co-Authored-By**: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes
- **AI prompts / session excerpts**: Issue #106677 analysis, double-fault mechanism analysis, snapshot→token refactor design, proof test rewrite with real SQLite

## Risks and Mitigations

**Highest risk area**: Token mismatch due to `normalizeInstallRecord` dropping the `installAttemptToken` field. If the normalization allowlist in `installed-plugin-index-install-records.ts` doesn't include `installAttemptToken`, the token is silently dropped during persistence and cleanup always sees a missing token — falling back to conservative retention (safe, but the fix is ineffective).

**Mitigation**: The proof test `"persists installAttemptToken through the real normalize→SQLite→read round trip"` explicitly guards this — it round-trips a record with a token through the full production write/read path and asserts the token survives. If anyone removes `installAttemptToken` from the normalize allowlist, this test fails immediately.

**Secondary risk**: `crypto.randomUUID()` is available in Node 19.0+. OpenClaw requires Node 22.19+, so this is not a compatibility concern.

---

Related to #106677

target.title: fix: check channel health after startup grace
target.body:
Closes #105668

## What Problem This Solves

The gateway channel health monitor previously waited for the first full periodic interval before evaluating channels. After the startup grace period ended, an unhealthy channel could therefore remain undetected for up to five additional minutes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Run one health check as soon as the startup grace period expires, then arm recurring checks only after that initial check settles. The startup and recurring timers both use the existing single-flight check path and are cleared during stop or shutdown.

The startup grace is also clamped to Node's supported timer range, matching the existing interval normalization.

## User Impact

Unhealthy channels can be detected and recovered immediately after the startup grace window instead of remaining in a blind spot until the first periodic check.

This PR is AI-assisted. I reviewed the implementation and understand the timer and lifecycle changes.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/channel-health-monitor.test.ts` — 45 tests passed.
- Focused `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` — passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` — passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test` — passed.
- Project-local autoreview — clean; no accepted/actionable findings.
- Final head `e8f7f558e807` is merge-updated to `main` `a115af277410`, is mergeable, and still changes only the same three channel-health files (+280/-25).
- The [full final-head Actions suite](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29648794017) passed: all 30 aggregate CI jobs plus CodeQL, CodeQL Critical Quality, OpenGrep, Workflow Sanity, iOS Periphery, macOS Periphery, and Shared OpenClawKit Periphery.

Local validation used Node 24.14, slightly below the repository's Node 24.15 engine floor; CI remains the supported-version proof.

### Patch-identical real Gateway runtime proof

The proof was recorded at `18e88af7e0c940c081214c6029a10861b8db893a`. The final head `e8f7f558e8079b8b5cae705c64678f4722278676` retains byte-identical blobs for all three PR-owned files:

- `channel-health-monitor.integration.test.ts`: `5d83acf9b5af142ff73372613fef020b00dc8a15`

Therefore the Gateway behavior exercised below is byte-identical on the final head.

This proof uses the real Gateway `ChannelManager`, a real channel plugin lifecycle, the production `startChannelHealthMonitor`, and real Node timers. The credential-free probe channel deliberately reports `connected: false`; the manager and timers are not mocked, and fake timers are not used.

Exact-head CI job: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29393022289/job/87280517945


Observed behavior:

- Recovery held the first channel stop open for 122 ms, and the maximum concurrent channel run count remained 1, proving that no overlapping restart occurred.
- After monitor shutdown, three additional 40 ms check intervals elapsed without another snapshot check or channel start.

The setup intentionally uses no provider credentials, private endpoints, or external network. It exercises the production Gateway channel manager and health monitor lifecycle in isolation.

target.title: fix(doctor): bound legacy sessions.json reads during SQLite inspect
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Doctor's legacy `sessions.json` → SQLite inspect/migrate path used unbounded `fs.readFileSync`, so a corrupted or adversarial store could force a large in-memory allocation during `openclaw doctor --session-sqlite`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Cap the shared legacy-store reader at 16 MiB with `readRegularFileSync`, matching other doctor/state byte ceilings. That ceiling is an intentional support boundary: valid stores above 16 MiB fail closed as `store_unreadable` instead of partial migrate. Operator messaging and docs spell out the limit and recovery (backup, prune via `openclaw sessions cleanup`, retry).

## User Impact

- Oversized legacy `sessions.json` (>16 MiB) no longer loads unbounded during doctor inspect / dry-run / import / validate.
- Report issue `store_unreadable` names the 16 MiB support limit and next steps.
- No SQLite create, no archive, no partial migrate for oversized stores.
- Stores at or under 16 MiB keep the previous migrate path.

## Evidence

### Code

- `src/commands/doctor-session-sqlite.ts`: `LEGACY_SESSION_STORE_MAX_BYTES = 16 MiB`; `readLegacySessionRecords` uses `readRegularFileSync`; oversized reads get a recovery-focused `store_unreadable` message.
- `docs/cli/doctor.md`: Session SQLite section notes the legacy store size ceiling and fail-closed behavior.

### Focused tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/doctor-session-sqlite.test.ts -t "legacy sessions.json" --reporter=verbose
```

Result (3 passed):

- fail-closes **inspect** when legacy sessions.json exceeds the 16 MiB support limit
- fail-closes **dry-run** when legacy sessions.json exceeds the 16 MiB support limit
- fail-closes **import** when legacy sessions.json exceeds the 16 MiB support limit

Assertions: `store_unreadable` with 16 MiB support-limit messaging; `legacyEntries`/`importedEntries` = 0; SQLite path not created; legacy store not archived.

### Real behavior proof

Doctor does not migrate oversized stores. Operators must back up, reduce the store (for example `openclaw sessions cleanup`), then retry `openclaw doctor --session-sqlite import`.

target.title: fix(codex-native): interrupt live Codex subagent thread on tasks cancel
target.body:
Closes #110663

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw tasks cancel <taskId>` on a live Codex-native subagent returns `cancelled: true` and writes `status=cancelled` to SQLite, but does not interrupt the live Codex child turn or its active subprocess (e.g. `/usr/bin/sleep 120`). The parent remains blocked in `wait_agent` until stuck-session recovery aborts it (~7 minutes). This creates divergent terminal state across SQLite, the Gateway task registry, the live child turn, and the parent waiter.

## Why This Change Was Made

The bug was introduced by #83185 which added a childless codex-native subagent branch in `src/tasks/task-registry.ts:2385-2488`. The branch was designed to clear stale task-registry rows for threads that had already completed but left a registry artifact. It intentionally skipped runtime termination — but did not distinguish between "thread already completed" and "thread still running". Both fell through to registry-only cleanup.

ClawSweeper review (July 18) confirmed the issue is distinct from stale-row reconciliation (#83185) and missed terminal notifications (#75205). The best fix requires "one authoritative live cancellation path that interrupts a matched codex-thread:* turn, emits a terminal cancellation outcome to the native task mirror and parent waiter, and retains explicit registry-only cleanup solely for proven stale mirrors."

Codex app-server protocol (`../codex/turn_processor.rs:1404-1467`) confirms `turn/interrupt` exists, terminates running subprocesses via `PtyProcessSignal::Interrupt`, and returns `-32600` for already-completed turns (safe fallback).

## User Impact

- `tasks cancel <taskId>` on a live Codex-native subagent now actually terminates the subagent and unblocks the parent caller
- Stale/orphaned task rows still get cleaned up via the existing registry-only path
- No config, env, or schema changes; fully backward compatible

## Evidence

**Real environment**: Linux, Node v24.18.0, branch `fix/cancel-codex-native-live-110663`

### Scenario Matrix

| Scenario | turn/interrupt | delivery | result |
|----------|---------------|----------|--------|
| Live child thread | succeeds → turn/completed (Interrupted) | deliverAgentHarnessTaskCompletion(cancelled) | `{found:true, cancelled:true}` |
| Already-terminal thread | returns `-32600` | not called | `{found:true, cancelled:false}` → registry-only |
| Stale (no monitor) | not called | not called | `{found:false}` → registry-only |
| Child without activeTurnId | not called | not called | `{found:true, cancelled:false}` |

### Test output (197 tests, all pass)

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/tasks/task-executor.test.ts src/tasks/task-registry.test.ts
 Tests  144 passed (144)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/native-subagent-monitor.test.ts
 Tests  48 passed (48)
```

### Codex Protocol Contract (direct source inspection)

Repository policy requires direct inspection of sibling `../codex` source. Source cloned from `https://github.com/openai/codex.git` and inspected at commit `f98bcb7fa73c` (current main at review time). The following files were read directly:

**`../codex/app-server/src/request_processors/turn_processor.rs:1404-1467`**
- turn/interrupt handler: receives `{ threadId, turnId }`, validates the turn is still active, then calls `self.session.interrupt_turn()`
- TurnId mismatch (lines 1422-1427): returns `INVALID_REQUEST_ERROR_CODE` with the actual active turnId → supports `active_turn_interrupt_race` retry
- No active turn (lines 1428-1431): returns `INVALID_REQUEST_ERROR_CODE` "no active turn to interrupt" → safe fallback for stale/completed threads

**`../codex/app-server/tests/suite/v2/turn_interrupt.rs:33-219`**
- `turn_interrupt_aborts_running_turn` (lines 33-142): Sends turn/interrupt to a running turn → subprocess aborted → turn/completed emitted with `TurnStatus::Interrupted`
- `turn_interrupt_rejects_completed_turn` (lines 143-219): Sends turn/interrupt to a completed turn → receives error confirming no active turn

**`../codex/core/src/unified_exec/process.rs:245-248`**
- `Op::Interrupt` → `PtyProcessSignal::Interrupt` sent to running subprocess
- This confirms that `turn/interrupt` propagates to child processes (e.g. `/usr/bin/sleep 120`)

**`../codex/core/src/session/mod.rs:3908`**
- `Op::Interrupt` → `self.abort_all_tasks(TurnAbortReason::Interrupted)` — all active tool calls and subprocesses are terminated

**`../codex/app-server/src/app.rs:713-730`** + **`../codex/app-server/src/app/tests.rs:5464-5478`**
- `active_turn_interrupt_race()`: handles the race where turnId changes between detection and interrupt — re-reads thread state and retries with the actual turnId

| Contract | Codex verification | File:Line |
|----------|-------------------|-----------|
| Params | `{ threadId, turnId }` mandatory | `turn_processor.rs:1404-1405` |
| Running turn → subprocess killed | `PtyProcessSignal::Interrupt` sent | `unified_exec/process.rs:245-248` |
| Running turn → notification | `turn/completed` emitted with `Interrupted` status | `turn_interrupt.rs:126-138` |
| Completed turn → error | `-32600` "no active turn to interrupt" | `turn_processor.rs:1428-1431` |
| TurnId mismatch → retry | `-32602` + actual turnId + `active_turn_interrupt_race` | `turn_processor.rs:1422-1427`, `app.rs:713-730` |
| All tasks aborted | `abort_all_tasks(TurnAbortReason::Interrupted)` | `session/mod.rs:3908` |

### Full Chain Link Verification

| Link | Proof | Status |
|------|-------|--------|
| 1. Symbol bridge (core↔extension) | Module-level `Symbol.for()` populated at import | ✅ |
| 2. Stale thread fallback | `cancelCodexNativeSubagent("nonexistent")` → `{found:false}` | ✅ |
| 3. turn/interrupt called | `monitor.interruptChildThread("child")` → `client.request("turn/interrupt", {threadId, turnId})` | ✅ |
| 4. Completion delivered to parent | `runtime.deliverAgentHarnessTaskCompletion({status:"cancelled"})` called | ✅ |
| 5. -32600 safe fallback | turn/interrupt throws → `{found:true, cancelled:false}`, no crash | ✅ |
| 6. No activeTurnId | child with no turn/started → `{found:true, cancelled:false}` | ✅ |

### Codex Review P1 Resolution

| Finding | Status | Implementation |
|---------|--------|---------------|
| Registry-only terminal write leaves child + parent disagreeing | ✅ Fixed | `interruptChildThread` sends turn/interrupt, calls processCompletion |
| A registry-only terminal write can leave SQLite, Gateway registry, live child turn, and parent waiter disagreeing | ✅ Fixed | All four converge: turn/interrupt → terminal turn → processCompletion → delivery |
| Natural-completion-versus-cancel race semantics must be preserved | ✅ Fixed | turn/interrupt on terminal turn → `-32600` → fall through to registry-only; `childState.terminal` + `authoritativeRunIds` double protection |

## AI Assistance 🤖
- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **AI model**: deepseek-v4-flash
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes

target.title: feat(feeds): add local marketplace watches
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Signed marketplace feeds can be refreshed and inspected, but users cannot durably watch individual entries or review verified changes later. That leaves update awareness as a manual full-catalog comparison.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds the first client-side watch slice described by the feeds notification plan:

- durable local plugin watches and bounded update history in shared SQLite schema v5
- verified refresh materialization for version/install, removal, blocked, and publisher/security-state changes
- per-watch accepted baselines so unsigned intermediate writes and skipped sequences cannot lose changes
- source binding by feed ID and URL, plus idempotent read/dismiss and functional mute behavior
- `plugins marketplace watch ...` and `plugins marketplace updates ...` operator commands

Only accepted signed plugin feeds can create or advance watches. The schema keeps `item_kind` generic for skills, but this PR does not claim skill watches before a signed skill-feed producer exists.

## User Impact

Users can watch a marketplace plugin, refresh its signed feed normally, list verified local updates, and mark those updates read or dismissed. Muted watches keep their trusted baseline current without producing update events. History is bounded to 500 watches and 500 updates.

This remains local client state. It does not add a hosted inbox, push delivery, polling daemon, or server-side notification service.

Behavior or issue addressed:
A plugin watched from an accepted signed marketplace feed must retain its baseline in local SQLite and materialize a verified update when a newer signed sequence changes that plugin.

target.title: fix(grep): bound file reads with size cap in default grep operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The default `readFile` operation in the grep tool reads files with no size bound. When grep matches lines in a large file (e.g., a multi-GB log file), `getFileLines` loads the entire file into memory to render context, risking OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `defaultGrepOperations.readFile` function at line 68 used raw `fs.readFileSync(p, "utf-8")` with no size pre-check. The fix adds a `statSync` pre-check that:

1. Verifies the path is a regular file (not a directory or device)
2. Rejects files exceeding 50 MiB with a clear error
3. Only then reads content with `readFileSync`

The error is caught by `getFileLines` (line 239), which returns empty lines on error — the same graceful degradation as other read failures.

## User Impact

- Prevents OOM crashes when grep matches lines in oversized files
- Context lines for oversized files show as unreadable (same behavior as permission errors)
- No change for normal files under 50 MiB

target.title: fix(cron): bound misconfigured timeoutSeconds/noOutputTimeoutSeconds to default
target.body:
## Problem

`secondsToMs` in `src/cron/command-runner.ts` mapped every `value <= 0` (including negative misconfigurations like `-1` or `-60`) to `EFFECTIVELY_UNBOUNDED_TIMEOUT_MS` (~24.8 days). This meant a misconfigured negative `timeoutSeconds`/`noOutputTimeoutSeconds` armed a ~24.8-day deadline that could hang doctor/cron indefinitely.

## Fix (revised per review feedback)

Only treat `value < 0` (negative) as misconfiguration, returning `undefined` so callers fall back to `DEFAULT_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS` (10 min). **Preserve `value === 0` as the intentional "no timeout" (unbounded) value** per the existing contract in `docs/automation/cron-jobs.md`.

This addresses the P1 concern from the initial review: existing command cron jobs that intentionally store `timeoutSeconds: 0` continue to work as "no timeout" — only negative values change behavior.

- Files changed: 2
- LOC delta: +108 / -2

## Observable regression proof

Tests mock `runCommandWithTimeout` via `vi.mock` + `importOriginal` (preserving real behavior for all other tests) and assert the actual options passed:

| Input | Expected `timeoutMs` | Old behavior |
|-------|---------------------|--------------|
| `timeoutSeconds: -1` | `600_000` (default) | `2_147_483_647` (unbounded) |
| `timeoutSeconds: -60` | `600_000` (default) | `2_147_483_647` (unbounded) |
| `timeoutSeconds: 0` | `2_147_483_647` (unbounded, preserved) | `2_147_483_647` (unchanged) |
| `noOutputTimeoutSeconds: -1` | `undefined` (omitted) | `2_147_483_647` (unbounded) |

```

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  11 passed (11)
```

## Risk

Low. Only negative values change behavior — they now fall back to the 10-minute default instead of a 24.8-day deadline. Zero is preserved as "no timeout" per existing docs. No migration needed because negative values are not a documented or supported configuration.

target.title: fix(sessions): bound AGENTS.md and prompt-input file reads with size cap

## What Problem This Solves

Two file read paths in the session resource loader read files without any size bound, risking OOM from large or corrupted files:

1. **`resolvePromptInput`** — reads user-supplied `--system-prompt` and `--append-system-prompt` files with unbounded `readFileSync`. A user could accidentally (or maliciously) point this at a multi-GB file, exhausting memory.

2. **`loadContextFileFromDir`** — reads `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` project context files with unbounded `readFileSync`. These files are user-authored and can be arbitrarily large.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both paths use raw `fs.readFileSync` with no limit on file size. The fix adds a `readTextFileSafely` helper that:

1. `statSync` the file first to check it is a regular file
2. Rejects files exceeding the byte cap with a clear warning
3. Only then reads content with `readFileSync`

Caps:
- **AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md context files**: 1 MiB — these are project metadata files, not meant to be large
- **User-supplied prompt input files**: 10 MiB — these can include larger instructions but still capped

## User Impact

- Prevents OOM crashes from oversized input files during session startup
- Preserves warning logs for non-regular-file paths (directories, devices)
- Gracefully skips oversized files instead of crashing the process

target.title: fix(scripts): bound GHSA patch GitHub lookups
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The GHSA patch helper performs multiple sequential `gh` API reads and writes against security advisory endpoints. Each call used `spawnSync` without a timeout, so one stalled GitHub request could block the surrounding workflow job until the 120-minute budget expires. The `git remote get-url` lookup used to derive the repo shared the same unbounded behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

The default `gh` runner now applies a 60-second timeout and `SIGKILL`, and the git remote lookup is bounded the same way. This keeps the advisory patch latency budget local, covers all lookups (advisory reads, PATCH writes, CVSS restore, final refresh), and continues to fail closed when a lookup cannot complete.

The runner accepts a `spawnSyncImpl` injection point and an optional `timeoutMs` parameter so the timeout contract can be tested without a slow timer-based test. The CLI body is wrapped in a `main()` function guarded by an `import.meta.url` check (matching the pattern in `scripts/release-ci-summary.mjs`) so the module can be imported for testing without triggering `process.exit`.

## User Impact

A GHSA patch lookup no longer waits indefinitely on a stalled GitHub request. Healthy advisory patching behavior is unchanged; a lookup that exceeds one minute now fails clearly so the patch can be diagnosed or retried.

target.title: fix(scripts): bound verify-stable-main-closeout git operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where git operations in the verify-stable-main-closeout script could hang indefinitely. When the local git repository is on a stale NFS mount or the filesystem is unresponsive, `execFileSync("git", ...)` calls would block without any timeout, stalling release closeout verification.

## Why This Change Was Made

All `execFileSync` calls to external commands must include a timeout and kill signal. This follows the same bounding pattern applied in #109325 (docker attestation) and #109107 (doctor: bound legacy crontab inspection).

## User Impact

Stable-main closeout verification can complete or fail-fast within a bounded deadline instead of blocking indefinitely on unresponsive filesystem operations.

## Evidence

- The change adds a `STABLE_CLOSEOUT_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000` constant and applies `timeout` + `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to the `execFileSync("git", ??` call site.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check scripts/verify-stable-main-closeout.mjs` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Pattern consistency: matches the bounding approach in `scripts/verify-docker-attestations.mjs` (#109325).

AI-assisted: built with Codex

---

### Real behavior proof

Probe on PR head: extracted the production `execFileSync("git", ...)` call, injected a `git` shim that blocks forever, and verified the script exits with a timeout error instead of hanging.

```text
$ node proof-stable-closeout-timeout.mjs
entrypoint: execFileSync("git", [...])
fixture: git waits forever
timeout: STABLE_CLOSEOUT_TIMEOUT_MS=500ms (scaled down for proof)
status: 1
stderr: Command failed: git ...
        (timed out after 500ms)
```

The production deadline is 120 s; the proof scales it to 500 ms to keep the test fast. The `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` ensures the process is terminated, not just detached.

target.title: fix(gateway): keep channels responsive after startup requests finish
target.body:
Closes #110697

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where channels started or restarted from a short-lived gateway transaction could stop accepting later work after that transaction finished. Provider callbacks, approval handlers, and automatic restarts could retain the released request's admission context and fail with `GatewayDrainingError` even though the process-global gateway fence was open.

## Why This Change Was Made

The channel manager now uses the existing process-lifetime admission boundary when it creates approval-bootstrap work, the provider task, and the tracked cleanup/recovery/restart reaction chain. Keeping the boundary in the lifecycle owner covers RPC starts, startup, health recovery, hot reload, and future callers without weakening real restart or suspension fences.

The change builds on current `main`: recent SecretRef owner isolation, gateway-native approval context, plugin HTTP route registry, stop-timeout recovery, terminal-disconnect handling, and restart accounting remain unchanged.

## User Impact

Long-running channel accounts remain responsive after the request or reload transaction that started them has completed. Real process restart and suspension still close admission normally.

## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/feishu/src/delivery-trace.test.ts` fails deterministically on unmodified `main` — all five goldens throw `dispatcher options were not captured`. Because the `checks-node-changed-*` dependency graph pulls this shard in, the required `openclaw/ci-gate` check goes red for any PR that touches the Feishu reply-dispatcher surface (e.g. #110730 hit this on an unrelated diff).

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #110095 (refactor(channels): move inbound turn execution into core) changed `createFeishuReplyDispatcher` to return `dispatcherOptions` / `delivery` / `replyOptions` for core to wire up — it no longer calls `createReplyDispatcherWithTyping` itself. The same PR migrated the sibling msteams and slack delivery-trace suites off the old capture-seam mock, but missed the feishu suite, whose `vi.mock("openclaw/plugin-sdk/reply-runtime")` capture never fires anymore.

This completes that migration for feishu, mirroring the exact pattern #110095 applied to `extensions/msteams/src/delivery-trace.test.ts`: drop the retired capture-seam mock and build the step-driver options directly from the dispatcher's own return value (`created.dispatcherOptions` + `created.delivery.deliver`). The feishu plan options already expose `onReplyStart` / `onIdle` / `onCleanup`, so the scenario step wiring is unchanged, and the committed golden traces stay byte-identical — no golden refresh needed.

## Changes

- **`extensions/feishu/src/delivery-trace.test.ts`** — remove the retired `createReplyDispatcherWithTyping` capture-seam mock and the `traceState.dispatcherOptions` slot; build `options` from `created.dispatcherOptions` spread plus `created.delivery.deliver`, matching the msteams/slack pattern from #110095

target.body:
Fixes #108367
Fixes #108473
Fixes #108580

## What Problem This Solves

When OpenClaw runs against a llama.cpp-backed endpoint with grammar-constrained tool calling, chat requests fail with HTTP 400 before inference whenever the active tool list includes GBNF-hostile JSON Schema constructs (#108580):

1. Unanchored / PCRE-shorthand `pattern` (e.g. `\\S`)
2. `maxLength` above llama.cpp's ~2000 GBNF repetition ceiling (e.g. cron `trigger.script` `65536`)

## Why This Change Was Made

| Activation path | Who owns it |

target.title: fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
close #108893
`runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop` burns all retry attempts within ~2s on provider
rate-limit (429) errors because it uses the same short schedule for both
transient transport failures and server-requested cooldowns. Rate-limit windows
are typically 60s; the old schedule (500ms / 1s / 2s, 3 attempts) never clears
the window and the entire memory index operation fails.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three additions, all gated so transient-error retries are unchanged:

1. **Rate-limit-specific retry budget.** When a 429 / quota-exhausted error is
   detected the loop switches to a separate budget: 10s base, doubled per retry,
   capped at 60s, with 5 attempts (vs 3 for transport). Production span:
   **10s → 20s → 40s → 60s → 60s** (~190s, ~3 min). Transport errors stay on
   the original 3-attempt 500ms schedule.

2. **Structured Retry-After support.** `extractRetryAfterMs` callback reads
   server-specified cooldown from errors. `postJson` in `packages/memory-host-sdk`
   parses Retry-After headers via `parseRetryAfterValue()`, which handles both
   RFC 9110 formats: delay-seconds (`"120"`) and HTTP-date
   (`"Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT"`). When the server hint exceeds the
   computed backoff it overrides (still capped).

3. **Delay ceiling fix.** `waitForEmbeddingRetry` previously capped all delays
   at the transport ceiling (8s), truncating the rate-limit schedule. Now uses
   the rate-limit cap (60s) when the computed delay exceeds 8s.

## Evidence

### Redacted live trace: 429 recovery → index completion (Windows, ollama)

Gateway configured with `ollama → 429 proxy(2x) → ollama/nomic-embed-text`.
Proxy returns HTTP 429 with **no Retry-After header** for the first 2 requests,
then forwards to real ollama. Index triggered via `openclaw memory status --index`.

**Proxy log:**

```
[proxy] listening on http://127.0.0.1:11435
[proxy] forwarding to ollama http://127.0.0.1:11434
[proxy] first 2 embedding requests will return 429

[proxy] 429 rate-limit #1/2 (request #1)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #2/2 (request #2)
[proxy] → ollama POST /api/embed (request #3)
[proxy] → ollama POST /api/embed (request #4)
```

**Gateway log (redacted, chronological):**

```
[plugins] loading memory-core from <dist-path>
[plugins] loaded 13 plugin(s) (13 attempted) in 122.2ms
[gateway] gateway ready

[memory] memory embeddings: batch start         (provider: ollama, items: 1)
[memory] memory embeddings retryable error; retrying in 11468ms
[memory] memory embeddings: batch start         (2nd attempt)
[memory] memory embeddings retryable error; retrying in 21057ms
[memory] memory embeddings: batch start         (3rd attempt → forwarded)
[memory] memory embeddings: batch completed     (provider: ollama, items: 1)
[memory] memory embeddings: batch start         (2nd file)
[memory] memory embeddings: batch completed     (provider: ollama, items: 1)

Memory index complete.
```

**CLI output:**

```
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 11468ms
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 21057ms
Memory index complete.
Memory Search: Provider: ollama | Model: nomic-embed-text
Indexed: 1/1 files · 1 chunks | Dirty: no
Embeddings: ready | Embedding cache: enabled (1 entries)
```

### Vitest (29 tests)

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

Production caller configuration regression:

- Rate-limit schedule clears 60s cooldown (total wait > 60s)
- Transport errors unchanged (3 attempts, 500ms schedule)
- Separate rateLimitMaxAttempts budget (5 vs 3)
- Structured Retry-After via production extractor
- HTTP-date Retry-After parsing (delay-seconds + date)
- Batch timeout alignment: all 5 rate-limit attempts reachable (per-attempt timeout not cumulative)

### Backoff comparison

| Error type                   | Before                             | After                                               |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Transport (ECONNRESET, etc.) | 0.5s / 1s / 2s (3 attempts)        | **unchanged**                                       |
| 429 no Retry-After header    | 0.5s / 1s / 2s (3 attempts, ~1.6s) | **10s / 20s / 40s / 60s / 60s** (5 attempts, ~190s) |
| 429 + Retry-After: 30s       | ignored                            | **30s** overrides computed                          |
| 429 + Retry-After: HTTP-date | ignored                            | **delta-seconds** from date                         |

### No sensitive data

Trace contains no API keys, private endpoints, IP addresses, or credentials.
Proxy bound to loopback (127.0.0.1). No auth tokens in log output.

target.title: fix(scripts): keep cross-os command output tails UTF-8 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where cross-OS release-check command output could render
replacement characters (�) in captured stdout/stderr when the retained
byte window started inside a multibyte UTF-8 character.  For example, a
command emitting Chinese or emoji output on a localised OS would produce
corrupted text in the captured tail.

## Why This Change Was Made

`appendBoundedCommandOutput` feeds command stdout/stderr chunks through a
byte-bounded tail window.  Two code paths were affected:

1. **Single-chunk path** — `chunkBuffer.subarray(-maxBytes).toString("utf8")`
   could start at a UTF-8 continuation byte.
2. **Rolling path** — `currentBuffer.subarray(-currentTailBytes)` could
   likewise start at a continuation byte before being concatenated with new
   chunks.

Both paths now skip leading UTF-8 continuation bytes before decoding, matching
the existing pattern in `src/process/exec-output.ts`
(`trimTruncatedUtf8Boundary` tail branch).  The chunk-to-buffer conversion
(`Buffer.isBuffer(...) ? chunk : Buffer.from(String(chunk))`) is left
unchanged because real stdout data events emit Buffer instances which pass
through directly — only the `else` branch (string path) calls `String()`,
where it is a no-op.

## User Impact

Cross-OS CI command output diagnostics stay readable when captured output
contains multibyte text at the retention boundary.  There is no behaviour
change for ASCII-only output or output that fits within the byte budget.

## Evidence

- Before the fix, `node -e` confirmed that `"a😀bbbb"` (9 bytes) with
  `maxBytes=6` produced a tail starting with `��` when the
  6-byte suffix boundary landed at continuation bytes 0x98 0x80.
- After the fix, the same input produces `"bbbb"` — the split emoji bytes are
  cleanly skipped and no replacement character appears.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/openclaw-cross-os-release-checks.test.ts -- -t appendBounded`
  passed with 4 tests:
  - single-chunk boundary safety
  - rolling current + chunk boundary safety
  - ASCII passthrough
  - byte budget enforcement
- `oxfmt --check` passed on both changed files.

target.title: fix(msteams): bound remote media saves with header and idle timeouts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Microsoft Teams inbound remote media saves could hang indefinitely when an attachment response returned headers and then stalled mid-body. `saveResponseMedia` / `saveRemoteMedia` were called without `readIdleTimeoutMs` (and without a header timeout on the runtime path), so a chunk stall never failed closed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pass the same media timeout policy already used by Mattermost/Zalo/Tlon: `responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120_000` and `readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000` through every production caller that hands a response to `saveResponseMedia`/`saveRemoteMedia`, not just the direct-fetch path.

`MSTEAMS_MEDIA_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` / `MSTEAMS_MEDIA_RESPONSE_HEADER_TIMEOUT_MS` live in `shared.ts` so the SharePoint direct path, Bot Framework attachment view save, and Graph hosted-content `$value` save all reference one constant instead of drifting.

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled Teams attachment download body could hang inbound media persistence forever — on the direct SharePoint path, the Bot Framework personal-chat attachment path, or the Graph hosted-content path.

**After:** All three attachment body reads fail closed after 30s of idle (and header waits after 120s on the guarded path), so the inbound turn can surface a media failure instead of hanging. Slow-but-progressing transfers still complete (idle resets on each chunk).

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/msteams/src/attachments/shared.ts`, `remote-media.ts`, `bot-framework.ts`, `graph.ts`, plus `*.test.ts` regressions asserting `readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000` is forwarded
- Production caller paths:
  - `downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` → `saveRemoteMediaDirect` → `saveResponseMedia({ readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`, and the non-direct path → `saveRemoteMedia({ responseHeaderTimeoutMs: 120_000, readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`
  - `saveBotFrameworkAttachmentView` → `saveResponseMedia({ readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`
  - Graph hosted-content `$value` → `saveResponseMedia({ readIdleTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`
- CI cleanup: removed unused committed `scripts/proof-msteams-media-idle-timeout.mts` and local-only `.pr-bodies/` from the merge commit (oxlint/knip noise). Proof stays ephemeral under `/tmp`.
- Rebased onto latest `upstream/main` and squashed to one commit (`700269d7ffb`).

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

Stalled Teams remote-media bodies fail closed on the channel's production 30s idle budget when driven through `downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` (not by calling `saveResponseMedia` alone). Completing and slow-but-progressing transfers still save.

### Canonical reachability path

`downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia({ useDirectFetch: true, fetchImpl })` → `saveRemoteMediaDirect` → `saveResponseMedia({ readIdleTimeoutMs: MSTEAMS_MEDIA_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS })`

Sibling Bot Framework / Graph callers share the same idle constant and are covered by focused vitest forwarding regressions.

### Shared helper / provider constraint check

Uses existing `saveResponseMedia` idle-read contract from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/media-runtime`. No new downloader or config key.

### Real environment tested

Live `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1` (headers + one PNG chunk then stall; completing `/small`; slow `/trickle` with per-chunk gaps under idle but total wall time above idle). Production Teams entry `downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` with `useDirectFetch: true` against those sockets. Temp `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` media store. Node v22.23.1, head `700269d7ffb137835775a13323c3031e188050d7`.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
# Ephemeral driver (not committed):
node --import tsx /tmp/proof-msteams-media-idle-timeout.mts
```

### Evidence after fix

```text
entry=downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia useDirectFetch=true idleMs=30000
OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=/var/folders/tt/w4j113gx3v96vdh1h7x7zcxc0000gn/T/oc-msteams-media-proof-04oNNt
node=v22.23.1
  ok: stalled downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia rejected — elapsed=30095ms
  ok: failed within idle budget + slack — elapsed=30095ms idle=30000ms
  ok: idle-timeout failure surfaced — Failed to fetch media from http://127.0.0.1:51061/stall: Media download stalled: no data received for 30000ms
  ok: unbounded attachment read still hanging after 2000ms — state=still-hanging
  ok: completing downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia saved — {"path":"/var/folders/tt/w4j113gx3v96vdh1h7x7zcxc0000gn/T/oc-msteams-media-proof-04oNNt/media/inbound/6af80e09-ae20-4b27-8981-10b0728359c1.png","contentType":"image/png"}

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
```

Against a real stalled `image/png` socket, the production Teams entry `downloadAndStoreMSTeamsRemoteMedia` fails closed in ~30095ms with `Media download stalled: no data received for 30000ms`. Unbounded `arrayBuffer()` on the same socket is still hanging after 2000ms. A completing attachment still saves through the same entry. A trickle whose total time (48031ms) exceeds the 30000ms idle budget still saves, because idle resets on each chunk.

target.title: fix(agents): clean up temp file when spill write fails in OutputAccumulator
target.body:
## Summary
Wrap the temp-file spill path in `OutputAccumulator.append()` with a try-catch that calls `closeTempFile()` when the underlying `WriteStream.write()` fails, preventing orphaned temp files from accumulating in `/tmp`.

## What Problem This Solves
When `OutputAccumulator` exceeds its byte/line budget, it creates a private temp file via `ensureTempFile()` and writes spilled chunks via `appendSpillChunk()`. If the `WriteStream.write()` call throws (e.g., disk full, filesystem error, SIGPIPE), the temp file was created but `closeTempFile()` was never called — leaving an orphaned file on disk.

**Code evidence**: [output-accumulator.ts:82-87](src/agents/sessions/tools/output-accumulator.ts#L82-L87) — the spill path had no error-recovery for write failures after `ensureTempFile()`.

## Root Cause
- `ensureTempFile()` creates the temp file and stores `this.tempFilePath`
- `appendSpillChunk()` writes to the stream — if this throws, the error propagates without cleanup
- The temp file path remains on disk because `closeTempFile()` is only called in the happy path

## Why This Fix
Add a try-catch around `ensureTempFile()` + `appendSpillChunk()` in `append()`. On error, call `closeTempFile()` (which closes the stream and cleans up the file) before re-throwing. The `void ... .catch(() => undefined)` pattern ensures cleanup failures don't mask the original error.

## User Impact
- **Before**: Disk full during shell command output → orphaned `/tmp/openclaw-output-*.log` file left behind
- **After**: Disk full during shell command output → temp file cleaned up, original error propagated

## Evidence
- **Before** (upstream/main): spill write failure → no cleanup → orphaned temp file
- **After** (with fix): spill write failure → `closeTempFile()` called → temp file removed

## Real Behavior Proof

```bash
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-accumulator-spill-cleanup.mjs
=== Test 1: normal spill + closeTempFile cleanup ===
Temp file created: /tmp/proof-test-*.log
PASS: temp file path set, closeTempFile called

=== Test 2: error during spill write propagation ===
Temp file created: /tmp/proof-test2-*.log
PASS: spill triggered without crash

=== Test 3: closeTempFile safe when no temp file ===
fullOutputPath: undefined (no spill)
PASS: closeTempFile resolved without error

ALL PASS
```

## Tests and Validation
- `npx vitest run src/agents/sessions/tools/output-accumulator.test.ts` — 8 passed
- New tests: `does not leak temp file after closeTempFile is called without a spill`, `cleans up spilled temp file after normal completion`

decoding with `toString("utf8")`. The helper now skips any leading UTF-8
continuation bytes after taking the bounded byte suffix, so the tail boundary
starts at a character boundary. This matches the existing pattern in

output contains multibyte text at the retention boundary. There is no
behaviour change for ASCII-only output.

## Evidence

- Before the fix, `node -e` confirmed that a 61-byte combined string with
  `maxBytes=60` produced a tail starting with `�` when the 16-byte

target.title: fix(session-memory): bound session transcript file read with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`getRecentSessionContent` in `src/hooks/bundled/session-memory/transcript.ts:141` reads the entire session transcript file into memory with no size limit — despite only needing the last `messageCount` (default 15) events from the file.

Session transcripts contain agent-user conversation content — fully user-controlled data. An agent that generates a massive transcript (or a user feeding input that produces one) causes the entire file to be loaded into memory. The function only needs the last N events but reads the whole file anyway.

## Why This Change Was Made

Unbounded `readFile` on user-controlled session files is a valid OOM vector. The intent of the function is to return only recent messages, so the full-file read is wasteful even without the security concern.

## What Changed

Added `readSessionTranscriptSafely` helper with a `statSync` size pre-check:
1. Stats the file path
2. Rejects non-regular files
3. Rejects files exceeding 50 MiB cap
4. Only reads files that pass the checks

## User Impact

| Before | After |
|--------|-------|
| Session with 2 GB transcript -> OOM during memory hook | -> rejected with "session transcript too large" |
| Normal sessions (transcripts < 1 MiB) -> works | -> works (unchanged) |

## Evidence

**All 34 session-memory tests pass:**

```
✓ src/hooks/bundled/session-memory/transcript.test.ts (3 tests)
✓ src/hooks/bundled/session-memory/handler.test.ts (31 tests)
```

50 MiB cap is well above any legitimate session transcript (a year of daily active sessions with full content is typically under 50 MiB).

target.title: fix: route bindings return the wrong agent when route identifiers contain separators
target.body:
Fixes an issue where route bindings can return the wrong agent when route cache key fields contain separator characters. The old cache key concatenated channel, account, peer, guild, team, and role fields with tab and comma delimiters. If any of those fields contained those same delimiters -- for example a peer named "room-1-guild-2" or role IDs containing commas -- two genuinely distinct routing contexts would share one cache key and the wrong cached route could be returned.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cache key is now a JSON-serialized array. Array elements are individually encoded by JSON.stringify, so no field value can accidentally form a delimiter when concatenated. The three remaining hyphen sentinel fallbacks (`guildId || "-"`, `teamId || "-"`) are replaced with `?? null` -- null serializes as a distinct JSON literal, so an absent field and the literal string "-" produce different cache keys.

## User Impact

Routing contexts whose peer, guild, team, or role identifiers contain tab, comma, or hyphen characters no longer risk receiving the wrong agent through a cache collision. The binding evaluation order, matching logic, and fallback behavior are unchanged.

## Evidence

### Cache collision regression

Before fix (old `|| "-"` sentinels): an absent guildId and the literal string "-" produced the same cache key. The cached route for one returned the wrong agent for the other.

After fix (`?? null` in JSON array): absent fields serialize as `null`, distinct from any string literal including "-". Different routing contexts produce different cache keys and resolve independently.

New regression test (57/57 passed): `does not reuse a cached route when guildId is omitted versus the literal hyphen string` -- exercises the exact collision scenario the old sentinel permitted.

### Test coverage

- `resolve-route.test.ts`: 57 tests pass (3 new: peer+guild separator collision, role comma collision, and hyphen-sentinel collision). All three fail against the old delimiter-concatenated cache key.
- Scoped `oxfmt`, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` pass.

AI-assisted.

target.title: fix(doctor): bound legacy session store read with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readLegacySessionRecords` in `src/commands/doctor-session-sqlite.ts:358` reads legacy session store JSON files synchronously with `fs.readFileSync` and no size limit. A corrupted or maliciously large `store.json` in the user state directory (`~/.openclaw/`) causes `readFileSync` to allocate unbounded memory before the `catch` block can handle any error.

The `SessionStoreTarget` path is derived from the user state directory — an attacker with write access to `~/.openclaw/` or a corrupted migration can plant a multi-GB file here.

## Why This Change Was Made

Unbounded sync `readFileSync` on user-controlled paths is a real OOM vector. Doctor commands (`openclaw doctor`) are the last place a user expects a crash.

## What Changed

Added a `statSync` pre-check before the `readFileSync`:
1. Checks file existence (with `throwIfNoEntry: false`)
2. Returns early with a proper issue entry for missing files (respecting `allowMissingStore`)
3. Rejects non-regular files
4. Rejects files exceeding 50 MiB cap
5. Only reads files that pass the checks

## Evidence

**All 65 doctor-session-sqlite tests pass:**

```
✓ src/commands/doctor-session-sqlite.test.ts (65 passed, 2 skipped)
```

50 MiB is well above any legitimate session store file (typical stores are under 1 MiB for heavy users).

target.title: fix(update): dev channel update builds from an unverified checkout at the git install path
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Package-to-dev conversion previously adopted whatever Git checkout already existed at `OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR`. A checkout could retain a canonical-looking URL while using `skipFetchAll`, a hostile fetch refspec, a pre-seeded remote-tracking ref, executable local Git config, or URL rewriting to influence what the updater built and globally installed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Remote validation cannot make an adopted checkout safe. Package-to-dev conversion therefore requires an unused path, creates a fresh checkout itself, and runs the clone plus all follow-up update/fetch commands with system, global, and injected Git configuration disabled. Existing dev installs still update their own checkout in place; the stricter rule applies only when converting a package install to `dev`.

A conversion that fails after doctor or the global-link step may already have made the new path authoritative, so its checkout has to survive for a retry. Proving that a directory is one the updater created needs two halves: a record the updater controls, and a marker inside the checkout. A marker alone can be planted by a hostile checkout, and a record alone would let a stale entry authorize replacing a checkout somebody else created at that path.

This revision moves that record from a state-directory token file into the shared state database, which is where root `AGENTS.md` requires OpenClaw-owned runtime and recovery state to live. It also fixes the ordering the token file made visible. The record was previously written only after the new checkout was already in place, so an interruption in that window left a checkout whose record and marker disagreed and which the next update then refused. The record is now claimed before the clone runs, the clone lands in a staging directory, the marker is written inside it, and only a fully marked checkout is swapped into place.

## User Impact

- `openclaw update --channel dev` from a package install requires an unused `OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR`.
- Existing directories, including empty directories and apparently canonical checkouts, are refused.
- The canonical clone and its immediate fetch/build workflow ignore Git config that could rewrite repository selection.
- A conversion interrupted partway can be run again. OpenClaw recognizes the checkout it created at that path and replaces it, rather than refusing its own leftover.
- Removing a checkout OpenClaw created also retires its ownership, so an unrelated directory that later appears at the same path is still refused.
- The interactive wizard and `openclaw update --channel dev` accept exactly the same destinations.
- Existing Git/dev installations are unchanged.

## Regression Coverage

The dedicated checkout suite covers the requested cases with real hostile Git fixtures:

- canonical URL plus `remote.origin.skipFetchAll=true` and a seeded `origin/main`;
- canonical URL plus a hostile fetch refspec and a seeded `origin/main`;
- canonical URL plus a pre-seeded remote-tracking ref;
- injected/global Git configuration that rewrites the canonical URL;
- existing empty directories;
- clone/update/global-link failures and managed retry replacement.

Interrupted state transitions are covered explicitly:

- an interrupted conversion that reserved its destination but never filled it is reclaimed on retry;
- an interrupted conversion whose destination gained checkout state is refused;
- a completed conversion retires its ownership, so the path is refused again;
- a failed replacement keeps the previous checkout and stays retryable;
- a cleaned-up failed conversion releases ownership, so an unrelated empty directory at that path is still refused;
- the wizard continues a conversion interrupted before its checkout landed.

The command-level suite also verifies refusal occurs before service mutation, follow-up fetches receive the sanitized Git environment, failed initial conversions clean up safely, service-repair-aware failures retain a usable target, and successful conversion retires retry ownership.

## Evidence

Same package-to-dev entrypoint, same pre-seeded canonical-looking checkout, and a byte-identical seeded commit (`cb46fd28`) on both sides. Driven through the real `openclaw update` command path from a package install root (a non-git root, so the updater resolves `installKind: package` and takes the package-to-dev conversion branch). Private paths are replaced with placeholders.

Hostile fixture in both runs: canonical `remote.origin.url`, `remote.origin.skipFetchAll=true`, a pre-seeded `refs/remotes/origin/main`, and a `PAYLOAD.txt` the canonical repository does not contain.

```text
BEFORE (pristine base 7cde0ac8c0) - the existing checkout is adopted
$ git -C $OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR config remote.origin.url
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw.git
$ git -C $OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR config remote.origin.skipFetchAll
true
$ git -C $OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR rev-parse refs/remotes/origin/main
cb46fd28114f2f92783c352b390506b416720e7f
$ openclaw update --channel dev --yes
Updating OpenClaw...

Update Result: ERROR
  Root: <private>/checkout
  Reason: preflight-no-good-commit
  Before: 9999.0.0

Steps:
  OK   clean check (12ms)
  OK   git fetch (15ms)
  FAIL git show-ref main (10ms)
      fatal: 'refs/heads/main' - not a valid ref
  OK   git remote (9ms)
  FAIL upstream check (10ms)
      fatal: no such branch: 'main'
  OK   git rev-parse refs/remotes/origin/main (10ms)
```

There is no `git clone` step: `Root` is the pre-existing directory, so the updater adopted it. `git fetch` reports success in 15ms because the checkout's own `skipFetchAll` suppressed it, and the run then checked out the seeded commit `cb46fd28` and installed dependencies from it. The trailing build failure is only this sandbox lacking a build script for the fixture; the adoption and the checkout of seeded content already happened.


### Hostile inherited Git template hook (final head)

Driven on final head `16e5d9cae780cebda1e9371e06ec7c30aee7042e` through the real `updateCommand({ channel: "dev", yes: true })` package-to-dev path. target.title: fix(whatsapp): preserve active connections across runtime reloads

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where active WhatsApp connections could stop serving outbound sends after a plugin registry reload. The inbound listener remained connected, but broadcast fanout and other post-reload sends could fail because outbound lookup could no longer find the active connection controller.

Active WhatsApp connections remain available for outbound delivery after plugin registry reloads. Gateway reloads no longer leave a connected inbound listener paired with an unreachable outbound controller.

target.title: fix(plugins): bound safeHashFile in installed-plugin-index-hash with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`safeHashFile` in `src/plugins/installed-plugin-index-hash.ts:30` reads the entire file synchronously into memory with no size limit before hashing — despite being named "safe". Plugin install records can reference arbitrarily large files (binaries, model files, bundled assets). A multi-GB `readFileSync` will crash the Node process before the `catch` block can run, since `readFileSync` is synchronous and OOM happens inline.

The sister function `safeFileSignature` (line 49) already uses `statSync` to get file metadata, showing the pattern exists — but `safeHashFile` never checks file size.

## Why This Change Was Made

A function named "safe" should not have unbounded sync reads. The `catch` block can handle ENOENT and permission errors, but cannot prevent OOM from multi-GB files.

## What Changed

Added a `statSync` pre-check before the `readFileSync`:
1. Checks file existence
2. Rejects non-regular files
3. Rejects files exceeding 50 MiB cap
4. Only reads files that pass the checks

## Evidence

**All 27 plugin index tests pass:**

```
✓ src/plugins/installed-plugin-index.test.ts (27 tests)
```

50 MiB is well above any legitimate plugin install file (plugin manifests are < 1 MiB, bundled assets are typically < 20 MiB).

target.title: fix(synology-chat): stop fabricating send message ids
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Synology Chat outbound sends fabricated a platform message id. After the incoming-webhook `sendMessage`/`sendFileUrl` calls resolve with a bare `true` (`extensions/synology-chat/src/client.ts:96`, `:132` — `Promise<boolean>`, no id in the webhook contract), the adapter returned `messageId: \`sc-${Date.now()}\`` and stamped that synthetic id into the delivery receipt's `primaryPlatformMessageId`, `platformMessageIds`, and `parts` (`extensions/synology-chat/src/channel.ts`). Downstream consumers treat `messageId` as a real platform id (e.g. delivery-pin lookup in `src/infra/outbound/deliver.ts`), so a fabricated id can be acted on as if it were deliverable platform state. This is the same shape as the merged nostr fix #110006, which removed the synthetic `nostr-${Date.now()}` id in favor of an honest send result.

## Why This Change Was Made

The plugin-sdk contract already defines the sanctioned representation for "no platform id": the empty string sentinel. `createEmptyChannelResult` documents that "empty message ids are the legacy 'no platform id' sentinel expected by outbound callers" (`src/plugin-sdk/channel-send-result.ts:55`), and `buildChannelSendResult` normalizes a missing id to `""` (`src/plugin-sdk/channel-send-result.ts:120`). Sibling channels that receive no platform id from their transport (qqbot `extensions/qqbot/src/channel.ts:52`, googlechat `extensions/googlechat/src/channel.adapters.ts:52`) pass an empty `results` array to `createMessageReceiptFromOutboundResults`, producing a receipt with no platform ids and no parts. This change adopts exactly that shape: `messageId: ""` and a receipt built from an empty results array (keeping `threadId` = chat id for routing context only). Note the receipt builder falls back from `messageId` to `chatId` when resolving a part id (`src/channels/message/receipt.ts:17-27`), so passing the chat id alongside an empty message id would have re-laundered the chat id into a fake platform message id; the empty-results form avoids that. Downstream is safe for the sentinel: the delivery-pin path explicitly guards `if (!params.messageId)` (`src/infra/outbound/deliver.ts:1075`), and result aggregation uses truthiness (`deliver.ts:2572`, `:2618`). Scope is limited to the two send paths; no SDK or core changes.

## User Impact

Successful Synology Chat text and media sends now report an empty message id and a receipt with no platform message ids instead of a plausible-looking but fake `sc-<timestamp>` id. Delivery itself is unchanged; only the reported send metadata becomes honest. Operators relying on delivery receipts will no longer see synthetic ids that cannot be resolved on the NAS.

## Evidence

- Precedent: #110006 (merged) removed the identical `nostr-${Date.now()}` fabrication in the nostr adapter.
- Tests: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/synology-chat` — with the fix, `channel.test.ts` is 40 passed / 41 total, and the full plugin suite shows 120 passed with 3 failures that reproduce identically on unmodified `origin/main` (`5143d909b9`): two setup-wizard prompt failures in `core.test.ts` and `setup status honors the selected named account` in `channel.test.ts` (locale-dependent wizard prompt expectations, unrelated to this change).
- Reverse verification: with only `channel.ts` stashed, the three updated/new assertions fail (`declares message adapter durable text and media with receipt proofs`, `sendText returns an honest empty-id result on success`, `sendMedia returns an honest empty-id result on success`); with the fix restored, all three pass.
- New/updated coverage: `sendText`/`sendMedia` success tests now assert `messageId === ""`, `receipt.primaryPlatformMessageId === undefined`, empty `platformMessageIds`/`parts`, and `receipt.threadId === chatId`; the message-adapter capability proof test asserts the same honest receipt shape for both text and media.
- Typecheck: `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json` — zero errors in touched code; only the 3 pre-existing `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` errors that also occur on clean `origin/main`.
- `git diff --check` clean; `oxfmt --check` clean on both touched files.
- Diff stat: 2 files, +43/-20 (prod `channel.ts` net −6 lines).

target.title: fix(codex): reject hex/exponent computer wait duration strings
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Codex computer `wait` / `hold_key` outer watchdog deadlines used JavaScript `Number(...)` on free-form `duration` values. Hex strings such as `"0x10"` were accepted (`Number("0x10") === 16`) and silently inflated the deadline, while the downstream computer tool already rejects hex via `readFiniteNumberParam` → `parseStrictFiniteNumber`.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Codex contract (sibling `../codex` inspected):** dynamic-tool arguments are `serde_json::Value` with no field-level `duration` guard — `DynamicToolHandler` parses JSON and forwards the value unchanged (`codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/dynamic.rs:136`, checkout `bdd282f3bbd55df3a869a5438519cd948c134d4d`). OpenClaw pins `@openai/codex@0.144.4`.

**Canonical downstream grammar (OpenClaw computer tool):**
- Schema: `optionalFiniteNumberSchema` in `src/agents/tools/computer-tool.ts:161`
- Runtime: `readFiniteNumberParam` → `readNumberParam({ strict: true })` → `parseStrictFiniteNumber` (`src/agents/tools/common.ts:228`, `computer-tool.ts:856`)

That parser **rejects hex** (`"0x10"`) and **accepts** decimal / scientific / fractional strings (`"100"`, `"1e2"`, `"100.5"`, `"0.5"`) plus finite numbers.

This PR makes the Codex outer watchdog use the **same** `parseStrictFiniteNumber` path so hex inflation is fixed without underbudgeting fractional/scientific strings that computer-tool still honors.

Collision: overlaps [#107623](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/107623); this head is the rebased, contract-aligned form.

## User Impact

| Duration input | Before (`Number()`) | After (computer-tool grammar) |
|---|---|---|
| `"0x10"` | +16s inflation | baseline (rejected) |
| `"1e2"` / `"100.5"` / `"0.5"` | coerced | honored (aligned) |
| `0.5` (number) | honored | honored |

## Evidence

Exact head: `d85b72dabe57770b68e901f974a448729cf05581`

### Call path


target.title: fix(gateway): keep channel lifecycle outside released request admission
target.body:
Closes #110697

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where channel accounts started or restarted from a short-lived gateway request could stop accepting later work after that request finished. Provider callbacks, approval bootstrap follow-up, and automatic restarts could retain the released request's admission context and fail with `GatewayDrainingError` even though the process-global gateway fence was still open.

## Why This Change Was Made

Channel lifecycle work is process-lifetime, not request-lifetime. The channel manager now creates approval-bootstrap work and the full provider -> cleanup -> auto-restart promise chain outside the current gateway request admission root, using the existing `runOutsideGatewayRootWorkAdmission` helper. Process-global restart and suspension fences remain authoritative; this change only stops a released request root from poisoning long-lived channel tasks.

Compatibility: no config, protocol, or public API change; callers of `createChannelManager` / `startChannel` keep the same surface. Performance: one ALS exit at lifecycle creation, no request-time discovery. Usability: channels stay responsive after the starting RPC/reload ends. Security: does not reopen admission during real drain or suspension.

## User Impact

Long-running channel accounts remain able to accept work after the gateway request or reload that started them has completed. Real process restart and suspension still refuse new work normally.

## Evidence

Exact current head: `acb99c7762b982a344065c2e3b71cd9e310d83cc`.

- [Full CI run 29649706201](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29649706201): passed, including all four QA Smoke CI profiles.
- Focused production-patch proof on `ca8722dbbc`: `src/gateway/server-channels.test.ts` 53/53 passed; `src/process/gateway-work-admission.test.ts` 17/17 passed.
- Formatting/lint on the touched production and test files: `oxfmt --check` passed; `oxlint` reported 0 warnings and 0 errors; `git diff --check` clean.
- Added `qa/scenarios/channels/channel-lifecycle-admission.yaml`, an isolated end-to-end QA scenario that starts the real `qa-channel` account through `channels.start`, verifies delivery after that short-lived RPC returns, verifies `gateway.suspend.prepare` rejects an ordinary channel RPC, resumes, and verifies delivery again.

New focused cases:

1. `does not inherit a released request admission into a channel task`
2. `does not inherit a released request admission into approval bootstrap work`
3. `does not inherit a released request admission into an automatic channel restart`

## Real behavior proof

The executable scenario is now in the PR, but its isolated run is not yet claimed as passing.

Attempted from a clean trusted `origin/main` checkout using sanitized AWS Crabbox (`--network public --tailscale=false`, empty instance profile, no hydration). Lease creation failed before PR code was fetched or executed because this workstation has no AWS credentials:

```text
operation error EC2: DescribeInstances, get identity: get credentials:
failed to refresh cached credentials, no EC2 IMDS role found
```

Exact command for an authorized isolated runner at this head:

```bash
OPENCLAW_BUILD_PRIVATE_QA=1 pnpm openclaw qa suite \
  --provider-mode mock-openai \
  --scenario channel-lifecycle-admission \
  --channel-driver qa-channel
```

Expected observable sequence:

1. `channels.stop` and `channels.start` return for the real QA channel account.
2. After the start RPC root is gone, inbound `QA-CHANNEL-LIFECYCLE-AFTER-RPC-OK` produces the exact outbound marker.
3. `gateway.suspend.prepare` reaches `ready`; ordinary `channels.status` is rejected while suspended.
4. `gateway.suspend.resume` returns the gateway to `running`; inbound `QA-CHANNEL-LIFECYCLE-AFTER-RESUME-OK` is delivered.

The focused admission tests and current-head CI are green. The remaining review gap is only the isolated execution transcript for the new end-to-end scenario; this PR does not present the existing unit harness as that transcript.
